title: Coats Disease: Clinical Masterclass
summary: Coats disease is a rare, idiopathic, non-hereditary condition characterized by telangiectatic and aneurysmal retinal vessels with massive subretinal exudation. It is a leading mimic of retinoblastoma and requires aggressive management to prevent vision loss and phthisis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Coats disease is an idiopathic condition (likely related to somatic mutations in the NDP gene) involving a breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. Abnormal endothelial cells and 'leaky' pericytes lead to the formation of telangiectatic 'light-bulb' aneurysms. This results in massive plasma and lipid leakage into the intraretinal and subretinal spaces, forming cholesterol-rich exudates and exudative retinal detachments.

sections.title: Parental Presentation: How it's Noticed
content: Leukocoria: A 'white reflex' or 'cat's eye' noticed in flash photography or dim light.
Strabismus: New onset eye turn (esotropia or exotropia) due to poor central vision.
Vision Loss: Older children may complain of blurred vision or 'bumping into things' on one side.
Nystagmus: Rare, but possible if bilateral or very early onset.
Red Eye: Noticed in late stages due to secondary glaucoma (painful red eye).

rows: Phthisis Bulbi or blind painful eye

branches: Chronic Total RD with Subretinal Fibrosis

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Telangiectatic vessels: 'Light-bulb' appearance of aneurysms.
Massive Exudation: Deep, yellow, subretinal lipid deposits.
Retinal Crystals: Glistening cholesterol crystals within exudates.
Retinal Non-perfusion: Areas of peripheral ischemia.
Exudative RD: Shiftable subretinal fluid, often inferiorly.
Light-bulb Sign: Focal dilations on the retinal venules and arterioles.

sections.title: Treatment: Management of Exudative RD
content: Step 1: Indirect Laser Photocoagulation: Ablate the telangiectatic vessels directly ('double-tap' or 'triple-tap' technique).
Step 2: Cryotherapy: Used for peripheral lesions or when exudation is too thick for laser penetration.
Step 3: Subretinal Fluid Drainage: External drainage via sclerotomy if the RD is too bullous for laser/cryo to reach the vessels.
Step 4: Scleral Buckling or PPV: Reserved for complex cases with vitreoretinal traction or non-resolving RD.
Step 5: Anti-VEGF Adjunct: Intravitreal Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab to reduce leakage and facilitate fluid resorption.

sections.title: Treatment: Macular Edema in Coats
content: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF: Rapidly reduces vascular permeability and ME (e.g., Bevacizumab 1.25mg).
Corticosteroids: Intravitreal Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) or Triamcinolone (Kenalog) to stabilize the BRB.
Grid Laser: Rarely used today; replaced by pharmacotherapy.
Peripheral Ablation: Treating the primary peripheral telangiectasia is mandatory to stop the 'source' of the macular fluid.

rows: Calcification on USG/CT; solid endophytic/exophytic mass.
Genetic, usually bilateral, straightening of vessels/dragging.
Endophthalmitis or focal granuloma with tractional bands.
Persistent stalk from disc to lens; microphthalmos.

content.explanation: C: Child (young male); O: Out-of-place (Unilateral); A: Aneurysms (Light-bulb); T: Telangiectasia; S: Subretinal Exudates/Subretinal Fluid.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Pathognomonic 'light-bulb' aneurysms and early leakage.
2. B-Scan Ultrasound: Shows SRF; crucially lacks the high-spike calcification seen in Retinoblastoma.
3. OCT: Quantifies Macular Edema and SRF depth.
4. CT/MRI: Performed if Rb cannot be ruled out (Rb has calcification on CT and T2-darkness on MRI).

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags
content: IOP Elevation: High risk of neovascular glaucoma.
Vitreous Seedings: If seen, strongly suspect Retinoblastoma instead of Coats.
Rapidly Progressive RD: May require immediate surgical drainage to save the globe.
Corneal Edema: Sign of decompensated glaucoma or end-stage phthisis.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a dilated fundus exam on the 'good' eye; though rare, bilateral cases exist and are often more aggressive.
Exudates can migrate to the fovea even if the telangiectasia is in the far periphery (gravitational settling).
The 'Yellow Reflex' in Coats is due to lipid, whereas the 'White Reflex' in Rb is due to tumor mass.
Aggressive treatment of stage 2 and 3A can often preserve ambulatory vision.
Serial Wide-Field Imaging (Optos) is essential for monitoring treatment response.
